belief: Counseling or medication shows a lack of faith.
meta: A Christian look at the false belief that counseling or medication shows a lack of faith, with Scripture, questions, and homework for replacing it with the truth.
origins: Hearing that Christians should “just pray more” instead of getting help. Distrust of psychology because some counselors dismissed faith. Fear of what others at church would think. Pride or embarrassment about needing help. Believing that if God wanted to heal you, He would do it without any human means.
teaches: God often works through people and practical means. Scripture praises wise counsel: plans succeed with many advisers. Luke was called “the beloved physician.” Paul told Timothy to take something for his stomach, and Isaiah had figs applied to King Hezekiah’s boil after God promised healing. Jesus said the sick need a doctor. Seeking good counsel and medical care can be an act of faith and stewardship, trusting God to work through the help He provides.
self_statements: If I had more faith, I wouldn’t need help.
Taking medicine means I don’t trust God.
Counseling is for people who aren’t right with God.
I should be able to pray this away.
People at church will think less of me.
Getting help means I’ve failed spiritually.
errors: Believing you must choose between trusting God and getting help.
“I should be able to handle this with prayer alone.”
Assuming everyone at church will judge you.
Accepting help for a broken arm but not for a hurting mind.
Ignoring passages where God works through advisers and physicians.
questions: Would I refuse a cast for a broken arm to prove my faith?
Why does Scripture praise many advisers if counsel shows weak faith?
Did Paul tell Timothy to stop trusting God when he advised a remedy?
Could God be answering my prayers through a counselor or doctor?
Is my reluctance about faith, or about pride or fear?
Can I pray and get help at the same time?
What would I tell a friend in my situation?
truth: Getting counseling or medication does not mean I lack faith. God often works through wise counsel and good medical care. I can pray and seek help at the same time, trusting God to use the people and tools He provides. Caring for my mind and body is good stewardship.
hw_questions: Would I refuse a cast to prove my faith?
Why does God praise many advisers?
Did Paul’s advice to Timothy show weak faith?
Could God answer my prayers through help?
Is this about faith or about pride and fear?
Can I pray and get help at the same time?
hw_truths: God often works through counselors and doctors.
Seeking help can be an act of faith.
I can pray and get help at the same time.
Caring for my mind and body is good stewardship.
The sick need a doctor, and that is no shame.
log: Each day, write one way God helped me through a person, a resource, or a treatment.
name_example: Sarah’s plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.
actions: to a Christian counselor or your doctor to ask about help.
Write down your fears about getting help,
then answer each one with a truth from this card.
Ask a respected Christian you know:
“Have you ever gotten counseling or medical help for your mind or emotions?” Listen to their story.
Pray before and after an appointment,
asking God to work through the help you receive.
tracker: One way God helped me through others
prayer: Father, thank You that You work through people and means to bring healing. Help me reject the lie that counseling or medication shows a lack of faith. Give me humility to seek help, wisdom to choose good help, and trust that You are at work in it. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
